The 1/𝒲1/\mathcal{W} Law: An Analytical Study of
Context-Length Routing Topology and GPU Generation Gains
for LLM Inference Energy Efficiency

Huamin Chen Affiliation: vLLM Semantic Router Project    Xunzhuo Liu Affiliation: vLLM Semantic Router Project    Yuhan Liu Affiliation: University of Chicago    Junchen Jiang Affiliation: Tensormesh Inc / University of Chicago    Bowei He ††thanks: Corresponding author: Bowei.He@mbzuai.ac.ae Affiliation: MBZUAI / McGill University    Xue Liu Affiliation: MBZUAI / McGill University
2026
Abstract

How many tokens can a GPU inference cluster deliver per watt? Across deployments of identical hardware, the answer varies by 40×\times—not because of software inefficiency, but because of the serving context window. We derive the 1/𝒲1/\mathcal{W} law: tokens per watt halves every time the context window doubles. The reason is simple: a larger context window shrinks the KV-cache concurrency limit while leaving GPU power draw roughly unchanged. At 64K context, an H100 can hold just 16 sequences in flight (tok/W =1.5=1.5); at 4K context, the same H100 holds 256 sequences (tok/W =17.6=17.6).

What operators often miss is that routing topology—which determines the effective context window each GPU actually services—is a more powerful energy lever than buying newer GPUs. Working from published H100 power measurements (Chung et al., 2026), a calibrated logistic power model (Liang et al., 2026), and a roofline throughput model (Xu et al., 2026), we derive these results analytically using the inference-fleet-sim planning framework (Chen et al., 2026b); no new hardware experiments were conducted. The analysis shows that two-pool context-length routing (FleetOpt (Chen et al., 2026a)) delivers roughly 2.5×2.5\times better tok/W over a homogeneous fleet on either H100 or B200, while a hardware upgrade from H100 to B200 delivers roughly 1.7×1.7\times at any topology. The two gains are independent—combining FleetOpt with B200 yields 4.25×4.25\times over the H100 homogeneous baseline, the product of the individual gains. Neither intervention alone gets you halfway there. B200 and H200 numbers are analytical projections (±\pm20% uncertainty); H100 results are calibrated to published measurements and carry higher confidence.

For MoE models, the model architecture itself adds a third lever. Using an active-parameter weight-streaming model, Qwen3-235B-A22B (22B active) on H100 reaches roughly 37.8 tok/W at 8K context analytically—5.1×\times better than Llama-3.1-70B—because the per-iteration decode time scales with the number of activated weights rather than the total. MoE dispatch overhead is excluded from this estimate, so the number is an upper bound; empirical measurements on real hardware are needed to narrow the range.

1 Introduction

Generative AI workloads now consume a measurable fraction of data center power, and that fraction is growing. Unlike batch compute jobs, LLM inference has a nonlinear relationship between load and power: a GPU serving a single request idles near 43% of its thermal design power (TDP), while the same GPU running a large batch approaches 86% TDP (Chung et al., 2026). The number of requests processed in parallel is therefore not just a throughput concern—it directly determines how much useful work you get per joule.

The main thing controlling how many requests a GPU can hold in parallel is the serving context window. A KV cache of fixed VRAM can hold fewer concurrent sequences as the per-token memory footprint grows. A Llama-3.1-70B deployment on H100 (80 GB, TP=8 with tensor-parallel KV sharding) (Meta AI, 2024) can hold 256 concurrent 4K-token sequences but only 16 concurrent 64K-token sequences. Tokens per watt drops by the same factor across those two operating points—roughly 12×12\times—and extends to a nearly 40×40\times spread across the full 2K to 128K context range.

GPU vendors have been responding to growing context demands with more powerful accelerators. B200 replaces H100 with 2.4×\times the memory bandwidth and 2.4×\times the VRAM—but also a TDP that is 43% higher (1,000 W vs. 700 W). Whether you actually get better tokens per watt from a B200 depends entirely on the context window distribution your workload presents at inference time.

This paper works out the quantitative relationships between context window, routing topology, hardware generation, and fleet energy efficiency. We connect three existing tools—the logistic GPU power model of Liang et al. (Liang et al., 2026) calibrated to ML.ENERGY measurements (Chung et al., 2026), the AIConfigurator roofline (Xu et al., 2026), and the inference-fleet-sim planner (Chen et al., 2026b)—to derive the 1/𝒲1/\mathcal{W} law (Section 3.1): tok/W halves every time the serving context window doubles, because halving concurrency halves throughput while power stays flat. This makes the context window—not the GPU—the primary energy knob.

From there we show (Section 4.2) that topology and hardware generation are independent levers. FleetOpt routing gives roughly 2.5×2.5\times over homogeneous on both H100 and B200; B200 gives roughly 1.7×1.7\times over H100 at any topology. Because the gains are orthogonal they multiply, reaching 4.25×4.25\times combined. Neither lever alone gets you half of that. Section 3.2 examines MoE models, where sparse activation collapses the per-iteration weight-streaming time and adds a third, architecture-level efficiency dimension.

2 Background

2.1 GPU Power Model

Liang et al. (Liang et al., 2026), studying GPU power as a knob for grid voltage regulation, characterized H100 power under LLM inference as a logistic curve in bb, the number of concurrently in-flight sequences (max_num_seqs in vLLM):

P⁡(b)=Prange1+e−k⁡(log2⁡b−x0)+Pidle,P(b)=\frac{P_{\text{range}}}{1+e^{-k(\log_{2}b-x_{0})}}+P_{\text{idle}}, (1)

where PidleP_{\text{idle}} is idle power, Prange=Pnom−PidleP_{\text{range}}=P_{\text{nom}}-P_{\text{idle}} is the dynamic range, kk controls how steeply power rises with batch size, and x0x_{0} is the half-saturation point. Chung et al. (Chung et al., 2026) provide direct measurements for H100-SXM5: Pidle=300P_{\text{idle}}=300 W at b=1b{=}1 and Pnom=600P_{\text{nom}}=600 W at b=128b{=}128, both within 3% fit error. The fitted logistic parameters are k=1.0k=1.0 and x0=4.2x_{0}=4.2, meaning power saturates around 24.2≈182^{4.2}\approx 18 concurrent sequences.

For B200-SXM, no published power-vs-concurrency curves existed as of March 2026. We apply the same TDP fractions validated on H100 (Pidle/TDP=0.43P_{\text{idle}}/\text{TDP}=0.43, Pnom/TDP=0.86P_{\text{nom}}/\text{TDP}=0.86) to B200’s 1,000 W TDP, giving Pidle=430P_{\text{idle}}=430 W and Pnom=860P_{\text{nom}}=860 W. Throughout the paper, we label H100 power estimates HIGH quality (directly measured) and B200 power estimates FAIR quality (projected; ±\pm20% uncertainty on absolute values).

KV-cache storage assumption.

Fleet results assume tensor-parallel sharding of KV heads: with TP=8 and Llama-3.1-70B’s nkv=8n_{\text{kv}}=8 GQA heads, each GPU stores one KV head, giving κ≈55\kappa\approx 55 KB/token. This matches the empirically calibrated H100 profile (nmax=128n_{\max}=128 at 8K context, implying 55 KB/token from the known VRAM budget) and is consistent with vLLM’s default behavior for GQA models. B200 KV capacity is then scaled proportionally by the memory-budget ratio—156 GB usable vs. 60 GB on H100—giving a 2.62×\times larger KV budget and nmaxB200≈2.62×nmaxH100n_{\max}^{\text{B200}}\approx 2.62\times n_{\max}^{\text{H100}} at any context window.

2.2 Token/Watt: Definition and Decomposition

Single-GPU tok/W.

For a GPU holding nactiven_{\text{active}} concurrent sequences with mean KV context length L¯\bar{L}, tokens per watt is:

tok/WGPU=nactive/τ⁡(nactive,L¯)P⁡(nactive),\text{tok/W}_{\text{GPU}}=\frac{n_{\text{active}}/\tau(n_{\text{active}},\bar{L})}{P(n_{\text{active}})}, (2)

where τ⁡(n,L¯)=W+H⁡(L¯)⋅n\tau(n,\bar{L})=W+H(\bar{L})\cdot n is the per-iteration decode latency from the roofline model. Here WW is the weight-streaming time per iteration (proportional to model size and inversely proportional to memory bandwidth), and H⁡(L¯)=H0⋅L¯/LcalibH(\bar{L})=H_{0}\cdot\bar{L}/L_{\text{calib}} is the per-sequence KV-scan overhead, which grows linearly with context length.

The maximum concurrency nmax​(𝒲)n_{\max}(\mathcal{W}) for a context window 𝒲\mathcal{W} is set by the KV-cache memory budget:

nmax​(𝒲)=⌊VKVκ⋅𝒲⌋,n_{\max}(\mathcal{W})=\left\lfloor\frac{V_{\text{KV}}}{\kappa\cdot\mathcal{W}}\right\rfloor, (3)

where VKVV_{\text{KV}} is the KV-cache VRAM after model weights and κ\kappa is the KV bytes per token. Since both nmaxn_{\max} and H⁡(L¯)H(\bar{L}) scale linearly with 𝒲\mathcal{W}, throughput at full concurrency scales as 1/𝒲1/\mathcal{W} while power stays roughly flat. This is the origin of the 1/𝒲1/\mathcal{W} law.

Fleet-level tok/W.

For a heterogeneous fleet of pools i∈{1,…,K}i\in\{1,\ldots,K\}, each with nin_{i} GPU instances:

tok/Wfleet=∑iλi⋅L¯out,i∑ini⋅P⁡(nact,i),\text{tok/W}_{\text{fleet}}=\frac{\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}\cdot\overline{L}_{\text{out},i}}{\sum_{i}n_{i}\cdot P(n_{\text{act},i})}, (4)

where λi\lambda_{i} is the request arrival rate to pool ii, L¯out,i\overline{L}_{\text{out},i} is the mean output length, and nact,i=ρi⋅nmax,in_{\text{act},i}=\rho_{i}\cdot n_{\max,i} is the mean in-flight batch at utilization ρi\rho_{i}. Fleet tok/W does not reduce to a single GPU-level quantity because nin_{i} and P⁡(nact,i)P(n_{\text{act},i}) vary across pools and must be weighted by GPU count.

3 Single-GPU Token Economy

3.1 Context Window as the Primary Lever

Table 1 shows how concurrency and tok/W change as the context window grows, for Llama-3.1-70B on H100-SXM5 and B200-SXM (TP=8, fp16). H100 uses the empirically calibrated profile; B200 values scale proportionally via the 2.62×\times KV-budget ratio from the roofline model (Xu et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026b).

The pattern in the table is striking. Tok/W halves with every doubling of the context window, for both GPU generations. This is the 1/𝒲1/\mathcal{W} law, and it is not approximate: doubling 𝒲\mathcal{W} halves nmaxn_{\max} (Eq. (3)), which halves throughput (since τ∝nmax⋅H∝𝒲\tau\propto n_{\max}\cdot H\propto\mathcal{W}), while power stays nearly constant. The GPU burns the same watts whether it holds 512 sequences or 8; the difference is entirely how much work it delivers per joule.

B200 shifts the curve up but does not change the slope. B200 achieves roughly 1.51.5–1.8×1.8\times higher tok/W than H100 at matching context windows, driven by a larger KV-cache budget (156 GB free vs. 60 GB on H100), faster weight streaming (W=2.95W=2.95 ms vs. 6.72 ms for 70B at TP=8), and correspondingly higher nmaxn_{\max}. But the halving-per-doubling relationship holds just as tightly on B200.

B200’s advantage narrows at long context. At 64K, B200 is only 1.49×1.49\times better than H100 (2.24 vs. 1.50 tok/W), down from 1.75×1.75\times at 4K. The culprit is idle power: B200’s Pidle=430P_{\text{idle}}=430 W represents a larger fraction of the total bill when nmaxn_{\max} is small (41 sequences at 64K vs. 671 at 4K). At 4K context both GPUs run near power saturation and the idle-power gap barely matters; at 64K a significant share of each GPU’s watt budget goes to just staying powered on. We return to the fleet-level implications in Section 4.

3.2 Model Architecture Effects

Table 2 compares single-GPU tok/W at nmaxn_{\max} across model families for an 8K context window.

Llama-3.1-405B is effectively unusable for long-context serving on H100 at 8K. With all 405B parameters loaded across eight GPUs in fp16, the KV budget is nearly exhausted by model weights alone, leaving room for only one sequence in flight. Tok/W is negligible because the GPU is spending most of its power just holding the model warm between sequential requests. B200’s additional memory lifts nmaxn_{\max} to 17, which is still modest but gives measurable efficiency. This model really needs hardware with large VRAM—B200, GB200, or a shorter context window.

The MoE numbers in the table warrant explanation. For Qwen3-235B-A22B, we override the default WW calculation to use only the 22B active parameters rather than the full 235B model. In a dense model, every weight is touched every iteration, so WW scales with total parameters. In a MoE model, only a small subset of experts is activated per token, so the weight-streaming time scales with the active count—roughly 22/235≈9%22/235\approx 9\% of a dense 235B model. This gives W≈1.6W\approx 1.6 ms on H100 (vs. 6.7 ms for the dense 70B baseline), which is why Qwen3-235B achieves dramatically higher tok/s and tok/W despite a much larger total parameter count.

The MoE values in the table are upper bounds, and the gap from reality can be large. Routing tokens to experts requires an all-to-all dispatch across TP ranks, which adds latency on top of active-weight streaming. Depending on network topology and expert load balance, dispatch can add anywhere from a few to tens of milliseconds per iteration. At 10 ms of dispatch overhead, the Qwen3 H100 advantage over Llama-70B shrinks from 5×5\times to around 1.5×1.5\times. The active-parameter estimate gives a principled lower bound on WW; empirical measurements on real hardware would substantially narrow the range.

Looking at B200 across models, the generation multiplier is anything but uniform. For sub-100B dense models it ranges from 1.6×1.6\times to 2.8×2.8\times, which is consistent with the bandwidth and memory improvements. But for models previously stuck at nmax≈1n_{\max}\approx 1—the 405B case—the jump is dramatic: from 0.09 to 2.16 tok/W, a 24×\times improvement. This happens not because B200 is fundamentally more efficient at that operating point, but because the added VRAM lets the GPU escape the near-idle serving regime where it was burning nearly PidleP_{\text{idle}} watts to deliver essentially nothing.

4 Fleet Topology and Token Economy

4.1 Fleet-Level Analysis Setup

When serving a production workload at a given SLO, an operator provisions enough GPUs to sustain the request arrival rate. Fleet tok/W depends on both per-GPU efficiency and the number of GPUs required—a topology that sends all traffic to a 64K context pool forces every GPU to run at the low-efficiency end of the 1/𝒲1/\mathcal{W} curve.

All fleet results in this section use Llama-3.1-70B (TP=8, fp16), sized to meet P99 TTFT ≤\leq 500 ms at λ=1,000\lambda=1{,}000 req/s. H100 uses the empirically calibrated profile with TP-sharded KV (nmax=128n_{\max}=128 at 8K context); B200 uses a profile scaled proportionally from H100 by the 2.62×\times KV-budget ratio (Section 2.1).

4.2 Topology Effects Across GPU Generations

Table 3 shows fleet tok/W for three topologies on H100 and B200 across two production workload traces.

The topology gain is consistent across both GPU generations. Define the topology improvement for GPU GG as tok/WFleetOpt​(G)/tok/WHomo​(G)\text{tok/W}_{\text{FleetOpt}}(G)/\text{tok/W}_{\text{Homo}}(G), and the generation improvement for topology TT as tok/WB200​(T)/tok/WH100​(T)\text{tok/W}_{\text{B200}}(T)/\text{tok/W}_{\text{H100}}(T). For Azure:

Δtopo​(H100)=14.08/5.58=2.52,Δtopo​(B200)=23.71/9.74=2.44.\Delta_{\text{topo}}(\text{H100})=14.08/5.58=2.52,\quad\Delta_{\text{topo}}(\text{B200})=23.71/9.74=2.44.
Δgen​(Homo)=9.74/5.58=1.75,Δgen​(FleetOpt)=23.71/14.08=1.68.\Delta_{\text{gen}}(\text{Homo})=9.74/5.58=1.75,\quad\Delta_{\text{gen}}(\text{FleetOpt})=23.71/14.08=1.68.

The topology gain barely changes between H100 and B200 (2.522.52 vs. 2.442.44), and the generation gain barely changes between homogeneous and FleetOpt (1.751.75 vs. 1.681.68). The two levers operate on different dimensions and don’t interact. That independence means the gains multiply: B200 FleetOpt delivers 2.52×1.75≈4.4×2.52\times 1.75\approx 4.4\times, matching the measured 23.71/5.58=4.25×23.71/5.58=4.25\times. Neither lever alone gets you close—FleetOpt with H100 gives 2.52×2.52\times and B200 with a homogeneous fleet gives 1.75×1.75\times, each less than half the combined improvement.

In practice, topology work and hardware upgrades are complementary investments, not substitutes. Operators who only buy better GPUs without rethinking topology capture 1.75×1.75\times and leave the other 2.4×2.4\times on the table. Operators who invest in two-pool routing on H100 capture 2.52×2.52\times and then can stack another 1.7×1.7\times on top with a future hardware upgrade—arriving at a fleet that delivers 4.25×\times better energy efficiency than where most operators start today.

5 Routing Topology Design Space

5.1 Context-Window Routing vs. Semantic Routing

The two-pool design in Section 4 partitions traffic by prompt length: requests shorter than BshortB_{\text{short}} go to the short pool (configured for a small context window), and the rest go to the long pool. An alternative is semantic routing: send simple or short requests to a small model (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B) and complex or long requests to a large model (e.g., Llama-3.1-70B). Table 4 compares the per-pool efficiency of the two approaches at ρ=0.85\rho=0.85 utilization.

The long pool is the binding constraint in both schemes. At 64K context, any model saturates at nmax=16n_{\max}=16 sequences per TP=8 group and delivers 1.52 tok/W—less than one-sixth of the short-pool value. When more than 89% of traffic is short-context (as in the Azure trace), the long pool is nearly idle yet still draws 413 W per group, dragging down the fleet average. The 1/𝒲1/\mathcal{W} law explains the magnitude: the 8×8\times context ratio between short and long pools implies 8×8\times fewer concurrent sequences, which translates to roughly 8×8\times lower tok/W. No amount of smarter routing eliminates this gap—it is a physical consequence of KV memory limits.

The choice between context routing and semantic routing is an efficiency tie for the long pool (both land at 1.52 tok/W at 64K) and a near-tie for the short pool (8.77 vs. 6.24 tok/W on a per-group basis). The 70B context-short pool appears more efficient per group because TP-sharded GQA allows more concurrent sequences (109 vs. 49). But on a per-physical-GPU basis, the 8B semantic pool wins: a single 8B GPU handles as many sequences as eight 70B TP-sharded GPUs combined, at a fraction of the cost. The bottom line is that the energy case for semantic routing depends not on tok/W but on whether the 8B model can satisfy output quality requirements for the short-context fraction of traffic.

5.2 Quantization Effects

Quantization to fp8 or int4 cuts weight bytes by 22–4×4\times (Micikevicius et al., 2022; Frantar et al., 2023), proportionally reducing WW. For H100+70B, fp8 gives W≈3.36W\approx 3.36 ms (vs. 6.72 ms in fp16), which roughly doubles tok/W at any fixed concurrency. The benefit is largest for dense models currently bottlenecked by weight streaming at moderate concurrency, and smallest for MoE models where WW is already small relative to KV overhead.

6 GPU Generation Comparison

Table 5 summarizes key hardware parameters and their impact on tok/W for Llama-3.1-70B (TP=8, fp16).

H200 is worth a closer look for Llama-3.1-70B at 8K context. It doubles nmaxn_{\max} over H100 (44 vs. 22) via 4.8 TB/s HBM3e bandwidth (1.4×1.4\times H100), cuts WW from 6.72 ms to 4.76 ms, and carries the same TDP and idle power floor as H100. The result is a 2.1×2.1\times tok/W improvement over H100 (15.58 vs. 7.41) at a rental cost roughly 50% higher.

B200 pushes further in absolute tok/W (20.93 vs. 15.58) by fitting still more sequences in flight (nmax=58n_{\max}=58 vs. 44). Higher idle power (430 W vs. 300 W) raises the power floor, but the 2.62×2.62\times larger memory budget more than compensates. On a tok/$M basis, B200 comes out ahead: 0.730.73M vs. 0.490.49M tok/$M/hr, because the throughput gain more than offsets the cost premium. At 8K context, B200 is the better choice on both absolute efficiency and cost efficiency.

GB200-NVL is a bit of a surprise. Despite having the same compute specs as B200-SXM, its per-GPU tok/W is lower (18.49 vs. 20.93) because the higher TDP (1,200 W per GPU equivalent) adds more power to the denominator than the slightly larger memory (200 GiB vs. 180 GiB) adds to the numerator. GB200’s advantage shows up not in this configuration but for very large models like the 405B or DeepSeek-V3, where its memory lets nmaxn_{\max} climb out of the near-zero regime.

7 Workload Archetype Effects

How much any topology helps depends entirely on the workload: the fraction of traffic at each context length determines how hard the long pool drags on the fleet average.

Short-context-dominant workloads (e.g., Azure).

89% of Azure Conversations requests fit within 4K tokens. The short pool handles nearly all traffic at high concurrency; the long pool is small and lightly loaded. FleetOpt on B200 reaches 23.7 tok/W—a +325% improvement over the H100 homogeneous baseline, composed of a 1.75×1.75\times generation gain and a 2.44×2.44\times topology gain that multiply to 4.25×4.25\times. This is the scenario where two-pool routing pays off most.

Dispersed workloads (e.g., agent-heavy).

In agent-heavy traces, 74% of requests fit within 8K tokens, but the remaining 26% extend to 64K (p99 ≈32\approx 32K). The long pool is large and dominates GPU-hours even with FleetOpt: a substantial fraction of traffic genuinely needs the long pool regardless of where you draw the split boundary. For these workloads, model architecture is the more productive energy lever—an MoE model with fast weight streaming benefits at every context length, not just the short tail.

Table 6 summarizes the recommended pairing of topology and GPU by archetype.

8 Related Work

The GPU power model at the core of this analysis comes from Liang et al. (Liang et al., 2026), who showed that GPU power under LLM workloads follows a logistic curve in batch size and that max_num_seqs is the primary control knob for grid voltage regulation. ML.ENERGY Benchmark v3.0 (Chung et al., 2026) provides the measurement data used to calibrate our H100 profile, and the AIConfigurator (Xu et al., 2026) supplies the roofline decomposition of WW and HH. We extend these single-GPU results to the fleet level and show that topology and generation gains are approximately independent and multiplicative.

On the inference systems side, Splitwise (Patel et al., 2024) introduced prefill-decode disaggregation, and vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) introduced PagedAttention for KV-cache management. Both optimize for latency and cost per token. FleetOpt (Chen et al., 2026a) and inference-fleet-sim (Chen et al., 2026b) approach the same problem from a fleet capacity perspective. The connection we make here is between routing topology and energy: topology controls which part of the P⁡(b)P(b) curve each GPU operates on, and therefore directly determines tok/W.

On the energy measurement side, Chung et al. (Chung et al., 2026) and TokenPowerBench (Niu et al., 2025) both confirm empirically that longer context degrades energy efficiency—TokenPowerBench reports roughly 3×3\times higher energy per token when prompt length grows from 2K to 10K on H100. That direction is consistent with the 1/𝒲1/\mathcal{W} law, but the mechanism differs: TokenPowerBench captures the cost of processing more input tokens during prefill, while our law governs the decode throughput ceiling set by KV-cache concurrency at a fixed serving context window. Maliakel et al. (Maliakel et al., 2025) show that the decode phase dominates inference time (77–91%) and is largely memory-bandwidth-bound, directly supporting the mechanistic basis of the 1/𝒲1/\mathcal{W} law.

GreenServ (Ziller et al., 2026) is the closest contemporaneous work on routing for energy efficiency. It routes individual queries across a heterogeneous pool of 16 open-source LLMs using a multi-armed bandit policy, achieving a 31% energy reduction over random routing. The shared intuition is that not every request needs the most expensive GPU or model. Where GreenServ and this paper diverge is in the mechanism: GreenServ routes across model families to avoid oversized models for easy tasks, while we route by context window within a single model to exploit the 1/𝒲1/\mathcal{W} law. The structural guarantee from KV-cache capacity yields larger gains (roughly 2.5×2.5\times at the fleet level) because context-window partitioning directly controls which segment of the logistic power curve each GPU occupies, rather than relying on learned query-difficulty estimates.

Routing topology as an explicit energy lever—distinct from model selection, quantization, or hardware choice—remains underexplored. Treating energy as a linear proxy for cost obscures the 1/𝒲1/\mathcal{W} relationship, which is multiplicative with hardware generation and independent of it.

9 Conclusion

Energy efficiency in LLM inference is shaped by three things that operators can actually control: GPU generation (which sets WW, PidleP_{\text{idle}}, and KV capacity), model architecture (which determines weight-streaming time and KV footprint), and routing topology (which determines the context window each GPU actually services). Of these, topology is the easiest to change today—you can restructure routing without buying anything new.

The 1/𝒲1/\mathcal{W} law explains why topology matters so much. Because tok/W halves every time the serving context window doubles, a routing strategy that confines short requests to a small-context pool effectively cuts the context window for the bulk of traffic. FleetOpt delivers roughly 2.5×2.5\times over a homogeneous fleet, and B200 delivers roughly 1.7×1.7\times over H100. These two improvements multiply, giving roughly 4.25×4.25\times total when combined— 2.5+1.7≠4.252.5+1.7\neq 4.25 because the gains stack on orthogonal dimensions.

MoE models have a natural tok/W edge from fast weight streaming—only the active experts get loaded per step—but putting a reliable number on that edge requires empirical MoE dispatch measurements that we do not have. The values in Table 2 are upper bounds.

All results are computed analytically via inference-fleet-sim (Chen et al., 2026b), with H100 power validated against ML.ENERGY v3.0. B200 numbers are projections with stated uncertainty. As measurement data for B200 and H200 becomes available, we expect the absolute numbers to shift somewhat while the qualitative picture— topology first, generation second, architecture third—holds.

10 Limitations, Assumptions, and Future Work

10.1 Modeling Assumptions

A few simplifying assumptions limit the scope of the results.

TP-sharded GQA KV storage.

Fleet results assume tensor-parallel sharding of KV heads, so each GPU stores nkv/TPn_{\text{kv}}/\text{TP} KV heads. For Llama-3.1-70B with nkv=8n_{\text{kv}}=8 and TP=8, this gives one head per GPU (κ≈40\kappa\approx 40–55 KB/token), maximizing nmaxn_{\max}. Models with fewer KV heads than TP ranks, or frameworks that replicate the full KV cache per GPU, will have lower nmaxn_{\max} and correspondingly lower tok/W.

Continuous-batching decode.

We model throughput as n/τ⁡(n,L¯)n/\tau(n,\bar{L}) with τ=W+H⋅n\tau=W+H\cdot n from the roofline. This is accurate for continuous-batching decoders (vLLM, TRT-LLM) in steady state. It does not capture chunked prefill interleaved with decode, head-of-line blocking, or KV-cache eviction under memory pressure. All three effects reduce achievable throughput, so the analytical tok/W is an upper bound.

Steady-state traffic.

Fleet sizing uses a steady-state queuing model at a fixed arrival rate, with context lengths drawn from a measured CDF. Real traffic is bursty and diurnal. Bursts require spare capacity beyond the steady-state minimum, which reduces average utilization and therefore tok/W. The reported values are attainable only under smooth, sustained load.

B200 power model quality.

B200 power parameters are derived from TDP-fraction heuristics calibrated on H100 data, then applied to B200’s 1,000 W TDP. No direct power-vs-concurrency measurements are available. We estimate ±\pm20% uncertainty on absolute B200 tok/W; the generation-gain ratios (≈1.7×\approx 1.7\times) are more robust because systematic errors partially cancel in the ratio.

Fixed TP=8, single model per pool.

All experiments use TP=8 instances of the same model in each pool. Smaller TP configurations are more power-efficient per GPU at low concurrency but reduce per-GPU throughput. Mixed-TP or mixed-model pools are not explored.

Output-only energy accounting.

Tok/W counts output tokens only. Prefill computation—which can account for 22–5×5\times the power per request for long-prompt workloads—is excluded. For workloads with prompt-to-output ratios much greater than one (e.g., document summarization, RAG), the reported tok/W overestimates true energy efficiency.

10.2 Limitations

No empirical validation on B200/H200.

The B200 and H200 results are projections. We have not measured vLLM or any production serving stack on B200 or H200, and cannot confirm that the power-vs-concurrency curve follows a logistic shape with the projected parameters. Researchers with access to these platforms should measure and publish the P⁡(b)P(b) curve to fill this gap.

Two-pool topology only.

FleetOpt defines a single split boundary with one overflow parameter. Real fleets may benefit from three or more pools partitioned by context length, or from content-adaptive pools that split on semantic class. The multiplicative gain structure suggests that finer-grained topologies could compound further efficiency improvements, but this is not analyzed here.

Static fleet sizing.

The analysis assumes a fixed, provisioned fleet. It does not model autoscaling, spot instances, or GPU sharing. In practice, dynamic scaling changes effective utilization and would alter the quantitative tok/W values.

Single workload CDF.

Each experiment uses one of two traces. Real deployments serve mixed traffic with time-varying CDFs. The optimal split boundary BshortB_{\text{short}} and overflow γ∗\gamma^{*} would need to be re-estimated as the workload shifts.

10.3 Future Work

Empirical B200/H200 power calibration.

The most immediate follow-on is measuring the logistic P⁡(b)P(b) curve for B200-SXM and H200-SXM using the ML.ENERGY methodology (Chung et al., 2026) and updating the fleet projections with HIGH-quality data.

Prefill-decode disaggregation.

Splitwise-style separation (Patel et al., 2024) assigns prefill and decode to different GPU pools. Combined with context-length routing, this could remove prefill energy from the output tok/W accounting and unlock further efficiency. Extending the power model to mixed prefill-decode batches is a natural next step.

Multi-pool topology optimization.

Extending FleetOpt from two pools to K≥3K\geq 3, potentially with different context windows and GPU types, could be formulated as a mixed-integer program. The multiplicative independence result suggests each additional split could compound the topology gain further.

Carbon-aware joint optimization.

Tok/W does not capture grid carbon intensity or electricity price. Minimizing $/token or gCO2/token requires accounting for PUE, time-of-day pricing, and grid mix. The per-GPU power model in this paper provides a natural starting point for a joint energy-cost objective.

Speculative decoding interaction.

Speculative decoding changes the batch-size distribution in the decode loop, potentially increasing average nactn_{\text{act}}. Whether this improves or degrades tok/W depends on the draft model’s power footprint and the verification hit rate—an open problem within the P⁡(b)P(b) framework.

Adaptive topology control.

The split boundary is currently fixed offline from a historical CDF. An online controller that monitors the live request-length distribution and adjusts pool boundaries dynamically could maintain near-optimal tok/W under distribution shift.

Appendix B Fleet Analyzer Code

All fleet tok/W results in this paper use the fleet_tpw_analysis API from inference-fleet-sim [Chen et al., 2026b]:

from fleet_sim.optimizer.base import fleet_tpw_analysis
result = fleet_tpw_analysis(
    pools=[
        dict(gpu=H100_80GB, cdf=short_cdf, lam=alpha*lam,
             max_ctx=B_short, label="short"),
        dict(gpu=H100_80GB, cdf=long_cdf, lam=(1-alpha)*lam,
             max_ctx=65536, label="long"),
    ],
    lam_total=lam, t_slo_ms=500.0,
)
print(result.fleet_tpw)     # tokens per joule
print(result.fleet_power_kw)

The API accepts any object satisfying the GpuProfile protocol (ManualProfile or ComputedProfile), which is what makes it straightforward to compare the measured H100 profile against B200 or GB200 projections on equal footing.
